"""Parse readings typed by technicians: '21.5C', '-4 F', '70f'."""
import re

_READING = re.compile(r"^\s*(-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*([CFK])\s*$", re.I)


def parse_reading(text):
    m = _READING.match(text)
    if not m:
        raise ValueError(f"bad reading: {text!r}")
    value, unit = float(m.group(1)), m.group(2).upper()
    if unit == "K" and value < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"below absolute zero: {text!r}")
    return value, unit

"""Group sales by calendar day."""
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import timezone

from store import all_sales


def daily_totals(sales=None, tz=None):
    """{date: total cents}, each sale assigned to its date in tz (default UTC)."""
    sales = all_sales() if sales is None else sales
    tz = timezone.utc if tz is None else tz
    out = defaultdict(int)
    for sale in sales:
        day = sale["at"].astimezone(tz).date()
        out[day] += sale["cents"]
    return dict(sorted(out.items()))

"""python cli.py [--title T] prints the daily sales report."""
import argparse
import re
from datetime import timedelta, timezone

from formatter import render
from service import daily_totals

_OFFSET = re.compile(r"^([+-])(\d{2}):(\d{2})$")


def utc_offset(text):
    m = _OFFSET.match(text)
    if not m or int(m.group(3)) >= 60:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"offset must look like +05:30 or -05:00, not {text!r}")
    delta = timedelta(hours=int(m.group(2)), minutes=int(m.group(3)))
    if delta > timedelta(hours=14):
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"offset beyond 14 hours: {text!r}")
    return text, timezone(-delta if m.group(1) == "-" else delta)


def main(argv=None, sales=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--title", default="Daily sales")
    p.add_argument("--utc-offset", type=utc_offset)
    args = p.parse_args(argv)
    if args.utc_offset:
        text, tz = args.utc_offset
        print(render(daily_totals(sales, tz=tz), title=f"{args.title} (UTC{text})"))
    else:
        print(render(daily_totals(sales), title=args.title))
    return 0

## Introduction

These notes cover every release of Quillmark Sync Server in the 5.x line, oldest first. Each entry says what kind of release it is, what changed, what was fixed and what an operator must do when upgrading. Feature release that starts the 5.x line. Introduces sync protocol 3, which replaces the polling protocol used by 4.x clients. Adds the setting sync.batch_size, which sets how many document changes the server sends to one client in a single sync round. Its default is 200.

Fixes:

- The comment threads releases file handles promptly after an upload is cancelled.
- The permission checker shows timestamps in the operator's configured time zone.
- The session manager rejects malformed requests before they reach the storage layer.
- The comment threads no longer drops changes when a client reconnects within a second of disconnecting.
- The comment threads retries transient storage errors with exponential backoff instead of failing the round.

# Brindlewick 2.x: installation and compatibility guide

## Overview

Brindlewick is an open-source background job queue for Python services. Producers add jobs to named queues; worker processes take jobs off the queues, run them and record the result. Brindlewick keeps its job records in PostgreSQL and can use either Redis or PostgreSQL itself to wake idle workers when new jobs arrive. This guide covers the 2.x releases: what each one needs, how to install it and how to move between releases.

## Compatibility matrix

The table lists, for every 2.x feature release, the Python, PostgreSQL and Redis versions it is tested against. Fix releases have the same requirements as the feature release they belong to, so 2.8.3 needs what 2.8 needs.

| Release | Released | Python | PostgreSQL | Redis | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.4 | 2024-11 | 3.9 to 3.12 | 12 to 16 | 6.2 or later | end of life |
| 2.5 | 2025-02 | 3.9 to 3.12 | 12 to 16 | 6.2 or later | end of life |
| 2.6 | 2025-05 | 3.10 to 3.13 | 13 to 17 | 6.2 or later | security fixes only |
| 2.7 | 2025-09 | 3.10 to 3.13 | 13 to 17 | 7.2 or later | security fixes only |
| 2.8 | 2026-01 | 3.11 to 3.14 | 14 to 17 | 7.2 or later | supported |
| 2.9 | 2026-05 | 3.11 to 3.14 | 14 to 18 | 7.2 or later | supported |

## Reading the matrix

A range such as 13 to 17 includes both ends. A version below the range is not supported and the installer refuses it. A version above the range usually works, but it has not been tested, and problems found on it are fixed only if they also occur on a tested version. Redis is needed only when you use it for wake-ups; with PostgreSQL wake-ups the Redis column does not apply. Status follows the support policy: supported releases get every fix, releases with security fixes only get those for twelve months after the next feature release, and end-of-life releases get nothing.

## Installing

Install Brindlewick from the package index into the same environment as the service that will produce jobs. Then create the schema with brindlewick migrate, pointing it at the PostgreSQL connection string in BRINDLEWICK_DSN. The command is safe to run more than once; it applies only the migrations that have not run yet. Start workers with brindlewick worker, naming the queues each worker should take jobs from. A worker with no queue names takes jobs from every queue, which is convenient in development but rarely what you want in production, where slow and fast queues should not share workers.

## Choosing a wake-up backend

Workers that find no jobs sleep until they are woken. With the PostgreSQL backend they listen for notifications on the job table, which needs no extra service but holds one database connection per worker. With the Redis backend they block on a Redis list, which scales to thousands of workers but adds a service to run. Choose PostgreSQL wake-ups for small deployments and Redis wake-ups when the number of workers would exhaust connections. The backend can be changed with a restart; no data moves.

## Upgrading within 2.x

Upgrades may skip feature releases. Run brindlewick migrate after installing the new release and before restarting workers; it applies the schema changes of every skipped release in order. Workers of the old and new release can run side by side for the length of a rolling restart, but not longer, because a newer worker may write job records an older one cannot read. Before upgrading, check the matrix: moving from 2.7 to 2.8 drops PostgreSQL 13 and Python 3.10, so those must be upgraded first.

## Known issues

2.6: workers can stop taking jobs after a Redis failover until they are restarted; fixed in 2.6.4. 2.7: the job dashboard shows durations in milliseconds while labelling them as seconds; fixed in 2.7.2. 2.8: retried jobs keep the priority of their first attempt even when the producer changes it; this is intended and documented. 2.9: none known.

# Ferncastle Payments Gateway: operations runbook

## Purpose

This runbook is for engineers on call for the Ferncastle Payments Gateway. It explains how the gateway is put together, the settings that differ between environments, the routine checks made every shift, and what to do first when each alert fires. It does not replace the incident process: if customers cannot pay, open an incident before you start working through this runbook.

## Architecture

Merchants call the gateway over HTTPS to authorise, capture and refund card payments. Each gateway replica is stateless; the state of every payment lives in the payments database, a PostgreSQL cluster with one writer and two readers per environment. Card numbers never reach the gateway's own storage: the gateway exchanges them for tokens at the card data vault, and from then on handles only tokens. # Postmortem INC-2291: delayed shipping labels

## Summary

On 2026-08-12, shipping labels for the Northline carrier were delayed for up to 47 minutes. Warehouse staff could pack orders but could not print labels for them, and 1,240 shipments missed their afternoon collection. The cause was a change in Northline's rate limits that our workers did not respect, so their retries kept the limit exhausted. No labels were lost and no customer was charged twice.

## Impact

Between 14:02 and 14:49 UTC, label jobs for Northline took between 4 and 47 minutes instead of the usual few seconds. Labels for other carriers were not affected. Of the 1,240 delayed shipments, 1,108 left on the evening collection and 132 left the next morning. Customer care received 61 contacts about late tracking numbers.

## Background

Pellbrook Freight creates shipping labels on demand. The warehouse packing screen calls the API gateway, which records a label job and returns at once. A pool of workers takes jobs, calls the carrier's API and stores the label. If a carrier call fails, the worker schedules a retry with a growing delay. A separate scheduler enqueues the nightly reprint batch for damaged labels and plays no part in creating labels on demand. This review is based on the gateway logs and the worker logs. The scheduler's logs were not collected, because the scheduler was not involved.

## Timeline

All times are UTC on 2026-08-12. The excerpt below follows one job, lbl-55120, and one neighbour through the incident; the full logs are attached to the incident record.

gateway 2026-08-12T14:02:41Z POST /labels 202 accepted job=lbl-55120 carrier=northline
gateway 2026-08-12T14:02:44Z POST /labels 202 accepted job=lbl-55121 carrier=northline
worker  2026-08-12T14:03:01Z job=lbl-55120 carrier=northline call started
worker  2026-08-12T14:03:21Z job=lbl-55120 carrier=northline status=timeout after=20s
worker  2026-08-12T14:03:24Z job=lbl-55121 carrier=northline status=timeout after=20s
gateway 2026-08-12T14:05:10Z GET /labels/lbl-55120 200 state=pending
worker  2026-08-12T14:07:12Z job=lbl-55120 retry attempt=1 backoff=240s
worker  2026-08-12T14:07:15Z job=lbl-55121 retry attempt=1 backoff=240s
worker  2026-08-12T14:11:30Z job=lbl-55120 carrier=northline status=429 retry_after=600s
worker  2026-08-12T14:49:02Z job=lbl-55120 carrier=northline status=ok label=issued

At 14:02 the gateway accepted label jobs as usual. From 14:03 every Northline call timed out after 20 seconds. Workers scheduled retries four minutes later, and when the retries ran, Northline answered with status 429, too many requests, and asked callers to wait ten minutes. Because every worker retried on its own schedule, the combined retries kept the account over its limit. At 14:31 the on-call engineer paused the Northline queue; the limit recovered, the queue was resumed at 14:41 at a reduced rate, and the backlog cleared by 14:49.

## Root cause

Northline lowered the per-account rate limit for label requests on 2026-08-11 and announced the change on its developer forum, which nobody on the team followed. With many workers retrying independently, the account never dropped below the new limit long enough to recover.

The gateway kept accepting jobs, so no label requests were lost and none had to be re-entered by hand. Pausing the queue was a single command and took effect at once. Warehouse leads moved packed orders to the evening collection without waiting to be asked.

## What went wrong

No alert fired. Our alerts watch the error rate of the gateway, which stayed at zero because the gateway itself was healthy; nothing watched how long label jobs waited. The first report came from a warehouse lead by phone, 22 minutes after the delays began. The retry logic had no special handling for rate limits, a gap noted in a code review last year and never scheduled.

Orders placed before 1 p.m. Eastern on a business day leave our warehouse the same day. Orders placed later, or on a weekend or holiday, leave on the next business day. Everything else, including news, tips and offers, is optional and can be turned off with the link at the bottom of each message or from the notification settings. The status page shows whether the Nimbrel Cloud Drive website, apps and checkout are working normally, and lists any problem we are investigating with the time it started and the latest update. You can subscribe to the status page by email to hear about problems as soon as we post them. We want everyone to be able to use Nimbrel Cloud Drive. Our pages and apps are tested with screen readers, keyboard-only navigation and high-contrast settings, and we fix accessibility problems with the same priority as other faults that stop people from completing a task. Text can be enlarged without breaking the layout, and every image that carries information has a text description. If something does not work for you, tell the Nimbrel support team: describe what you were trying to do and which device and assistive technology you use, and we will reply with a fix or a way around the problem.

The community forum is a place to ask questions, share tips and suggest improvements. Answers in the forum come from other customers as often as from staff. If you no longer have access to the email address on your account, contact the Nimbrel support team, who will ask a few questions to confirm that the account is yours before changing anything.

# Gildercrest Hosting: scheduled maintenance

## What maintenance covers

Gildercrest Hosting applies operating system patches, hypervisor updates and network changes to its regions during scheduled maintenance windows. Most maintenance causes no interruption, because virtual machines are moved to updated hosts while they keep running. Some changes need a restart: when they do, the restart happens inside the window and the notice lists the affected machines.

## Weekly windows

Each region has one weekly window, chosen to fall in the quiet hours of the region's customers. The table gives each window in UTC and how far ahead maintenance in it is announced.

| Region | Weekly window (UTC) | Notice given |
|---|---|---|
| US-East | Sunday 06:00 to 08:00 | 5 days |
| US-West | Sunday 09:00 to 11:00 [1] | 5 days |
| EU-West | Sunday 02:00 to 04:00 [2] | 5 days |
| AP-South | Saturday 20:00 to 22:00 | 7 days |

[1] US-West windows may run up to 30 minutes over when a storage firmware update is included. The notice says when this applies.

[2] From the last Sunday in March to the last Sunday in October, the EU-West window starts an hour earlier, at 01:00 UTC, and ends at 03:00 UTC, so that it stays at the same local time all year.

## Notice and notifications

Maintenance that may affect your machines is announced by email to the account's technical contacts and on the status page, with the notice period shown in the table. The notice names the region, the window, the kind of change, and the machines that will restart, if any. If a window is not needed in a given week, no notice is sent and nothing happens.

## During a window

Live migration pauses a machine for less than a second, which most applications do not notice. Machines that need a restart are stopped cleanly, restarted on an updated host and returned to the state they were in. Load balancers drain traffic from a machine before it restarts if the machine is in a health-checked pool. The status page shows progress while a window is under way and marks it complete when it ends.

## Emergency maintenance

A security problem that is being exploited, or a fault that threatens customer data, may need maintenance outside the weekly windows. Emergency maintenance is announced as early as possible, at least one hour ahead when that is safe, and the announcement explains why it could not wait for the next window.

## Deferring maintenance

Customers on the Enterprise plan can defer a scheduled restart of their machines once per quarter, by up to seven days, from the maintenance page. A deferred restart happens in the region's next window. Security updates cannot be deferred.

## About this document

This document is maintained by the infrastructure operations team and is reviewed at least once a quarter. It describes Gildercrest Hosting as it is deployed and supported today; it is not a design proposal and it does not describe work that has not shipped. Where this document and an older wiki page disagree, this document wins, and the wiki page should be reported so that it can be corrected or archived. Comments and corrections go to the infrastructure operations team through the usual request queue. Section headings are stable, so links to them from other documents keep working when the text underneath changes. Terms that have a specific meaning here are defined in the glossary near the end.

## Support and escalation

Questions about Gildercrest Hosting go first to the infrastructure operations team request queue, which is watched during business hours. A request is acknowledged within four business hours and gets a first substantive answer within two business days. Anything that blocks customers counts as an incident rather than a request: open an incident through the incident tool, which pages the on-call engineer directly, instead of filing a queue item and waiting. When you escalate, include what you expected to happen, what happened instead, the time it started and anything you have already tried. Screenshots help, but paste error text as text so that it can be searched. Please do not message individual engineers about production problems; the queue and the incident tool keep a record that the next person on shift can read.

## Change management

Every change to Gildercrest Hosting goes through a reviewed pull request and a change record. Routine changes, such as a dependency bump with passing tests, need one reviewer. Changes that alter behaviour customers can see need two reviewers, one of them from outside the authoring team, and a short note in the change record describing how to undo the change. Changes are not deployed on Friday afternoons or during company-wide freeze periods, which are announced at least two weeks ahead. Emergency fixes may skip the waiting period, but they still need a reviewer and a change record written within one business day. The change record links the pull request, the deployment and any incident that prompted the change, so that someone reading it later can follow the whole story.

## Glossary

Operator: a person with permission to change the running configuration. Tenant: one customer account, together with all of its users and data. Release: a numbered, tagged build that has passed the full test suite. Rollback: returning to the previous release, as opposed to fixing forward with a new one. Request queue: the ticketing queue owned by the infrastructure operations team. Business day: Monday to Friday, excluding company holidays. Change record: the short written summary that accompanies every deployed change. On-call engineer: the person currently holding the pager for Gildercrest Hosting.

## Feedback

Suggestions for improving Gildercrest Hosting are welcome at any time. The infrastructure operations team reviews the suggestion board every two weeks, groups related items, and replies to each one with a decision: planned, considered for later, or declined with a reason. Planned items are linked to the work tracker so that the person who suggested them can follow progress. When a suggestion is declined, the reply explains what would need to change for it to be reconsidered. Please search the board before adding a new suggestion; a comment on an existing item helps more than a duplicate.

## Training and onboarding

New members of the infrastructure operations team spend their first two weeks shadowing the on-call rotation before they take a shift of their own. The onboarding checklist covers the architecture walkthrough, the local development setup, a supervised deployment, and a tabletop exercise in which the new engineer works through a recorded incident from start to finish. Recorded walkthroughs are kept in the team's video library and are refreshed whenever the architecture changes in a way that makes them misleading. People outside the team who use Gildercrest Hosting regularly are welcome at the monthly open office hours, where the team answers questions and demonstrates recent changes.

## On-call rotation

The infrastructure operations team runs a weekly on-call rotation that changes over on Monday mornings. The engineer coming off call writes a handover note listing open incidents, anything that paged more than once, and work left half done. The engineer going on call reads it before taking the pager and asks questions while the previous engineer is still around to answer them. Each shift has a primary and a secondary; the secondary takes pages the primary cannot acknowledge in time and covers short absences. Swaps are fine as long as both people agree and the rotation tool is updated before the swap begins, so that pages reach the right phone. Nobody is on call two weeks running unless they ask to be.

## Writing documentation

Documentation for Gildercrest Hosting lives next to the code and is reviewed in the same pull requests. A change that alters behaviour must update the documents that describe that behaviour, or explain in the pull request why none do. Runbooks are written for a tired engineer at night: short steps, the exact commands to run, and what the output should look like. Each document names its owner and the date it was last checked. Documents that have not been checked for a year are flagged on the team's board and either refreshed or archived.

## Deprecation policy

Features of Gildercrest Hosting are deprecated before they are removed. A deprecation is announced in the release notes and in the announcements channel, together with the replacement and a removal date at least two releases away. During the deprecation period the old behaviour keeps working but logs a warning each time it is used, so that owners of dependent systems can find their remaining uses. The infrastructure operations team contacts the owners of any system still using a deprecated feature one month before removal. Removal dates move only later, never earlier, unless a security problem makes the old behaviour unsafe to keep.

## Cost reporting

The running cost of Gildercrest Hosting is reported every month, broken down by component and by environment. The report shows the change since the previous month and explains any change larger than ten percent. Costs that cannot be assigned to one component, such as shared networking, are split by usage. The infrastructure operations team looks for savings twice a year: unused resources, oversized machines and storage that nobody reads any more. Savings that need a design change go into the normal planning process rather than being made in a hurry, because the cheapest configuration is not always the one that keeps working under load.

## Incident process

An incident is any event that stops customers from using Gildercrest Hosting as they expect, or that puts data at risk. The first person to notice opens an incident in the incident tool, which creates a chat room and pages the on-call engineer. One person acts as incident lead and keeps a running log of what was seen and what was tried; other people work on the problem and report back to the lead rather than acting on their own. Customer-facing updates go out through the status page, written by the lead or someone they name. When the incident is over, the lead schedules a review within five business days. Reviews look for causes in systems and processes, not in individual people.
